articles.title: The 37th pair breaks the six-entry rulebook
articles.dek: Lean checked the exact capacity. Four hidden switches and six entries per rule can handle 36 pairs of lights. A 37th pair forces a longer rule.

articles.title: Flip the rule and read the whole table
articles.dek: Lean checked that nonempty clauses covering every switch admit blocked patterns whose common flips recover a whole table from sums.

articles.title: One extra sensor takes a choice off the menu
articles.dek: Lean checked that a shared menu of three patterns identifies two hidden strips using five row end sensors and four column end sensors.

articles.title: Shorter rules can make a longer rulebook
articles.dek: Lean checked that detecting a fully lit pair among 36 pairs needs 88 clauses with four hidden switches and a six-entry limit.

articles.title: How short can a rulebook be when each rule must be short too?
articles.dek: Lean checked when a rulebook can tell whether any pair of lights is fully on, while meeting limits on rule count and rule length.

articles.title: The circuit wire that comes for free
articles.dek: Lean checked when an extra pair of switches costs two gates, one gate, or zero, depending on the answers the circuit must keep.

articles.title: Why sixteen reports can need 32,768 keys
articles.dek: Keeping 16 reports equally likely under every allowed sensor rule can take a fixed sample of 32,768 keys with equal weights.

articles.title: The colours one gate can see
articles.dek: With parity and NOT free, one two-input AND or OR gate fits every label in this switch test exactly when three colours can separate every linked pair.

articles.title: The message hiding in the pairs
articles.dek: Eight messages share the same completion counts and red-mismatch sums on a 60-light ring. Counting pairs of red mismatches recovers all three bits.

articles.title: Three blanks turn 201 gates into six
articles.dek: With one row and column lit, a 100-by-100 board with three diagonal blanks needs 201 AND/OR gates or six with one NOT. Each gate reads at most two wires.

articles.title: Guess now or find out for sure
articles.dek: A cheapest parity-question strategy at thirteen wins in sixteen in this four-switch game mixes immediate guesses with exact play.

articles.title: The hidden strips a second look still cannot tell apart
articles.dek: Lean checked two limits on a four-sensor follow-up. A fixed scan falls short of its target, and an adaptive scan still leaves a collision.

articles.title: The extra input that changed wire two
articles.dek: Lean checked that an AND/OR circuit keeps a true output when equal-length inputs only change bits from false to true.

articles.title: The only multiplier this test misses is 97
articles.dek: The checked two-pair test in a 512-element field detects 510 of 511 nonzero multipliers. The one it misses is 97.

articles.title: When every nonzero choice can be detected
articles.dek: In a 128-element field, a checked two-pair matrix construction detects all 127 nonzero inputs. Only zero makes all three tests vanish.

articles.title: When four corners stop being fair
articles.dek: On a nine-by-nine board with one nonlinear layer, four corners give a biased odd-or-even count with three nonlinear gates to spend, and a fair count with four.

articles.title: The twelfth report closes the cycle
articles.dek: Any eleven requested bits fit on the checked twelve-input sensor cycle. All twelve fit exactly when their total is even.

articles.title: All 255 nonzero inputs show up
articles.dek: Three grouped matrix tests detect every nonzero input in the checked 256-element field construction. All three vanish together only at zero.

articles.title: The light that saves a question
articles.dek: On this switch ring, three fixed questions identify the reply table. With three lights per reply, one bit of feedback makes two enough.

articles.title: Twelve readings for 1,024 hidden weights
articles.dek: Ten separate two-by-two blocks have 1,024 matching weights. Twelve determinant readings recover them all. Even with feedback, eleven cannot guarantee it.

articles.title: 493 graphs, one answer: a single NOT gate saved nothing
articles.dek: One question, 500 graphs, both sides posted. By 19:51 UTC contributors had decided 493 in Lean, all one way: one NOT gate saves nothing.

articles.title: The crowd said thirteen circuits could not exist. Lean agrees.
articles.dek: Contributors kept reporting that thirteen small circuits could not exist. Lean has now checked all thirteen impossibility statements.

articles.title: Fifty-five minutes from a filed statement to a checked floor
articles.dek: Fifty-five minutes from filing to Lean: on one-row, one-column inputs, a gate floor was checked for fan-in-two circuits even with NOT gates.

articles.title: Why 255 edits cannot flatten this table
articles.dek: If each pair of rows in a 64-by-64 table of signs agrees in 32 places, making every row a weighted sum of four patterns takes at least 256 edits.

articles.title: Why forty lights need 524,288 checklists
articles.dek: It takes exactly 524,288 checklists to recognize an odd number of lit lights out of forty when each line allows at most two on-or-off conditions.

articles.title: When guessing no is as good as it gets
articles.dek: On this six-switch puzzle, always guessing no scores 50 out of 64, the most any quadratic rule can get even if it reads every switch.

articles.title: Six lights, exactly six gates
articles.dek: There are just four ways to win the six-light puzzle, yet every five-gate AND/OR/NOT circuit with at most two inputs per gate gets a legal setting wrong.

articles.title: Can an odd-or-even gate count the ways around a ring?
articles.dek: Even with odd-or-even gates, polynomial-size AND/OR/NOT circuits of fixed depth cannot test every ring for an odd number of settings obeying its pair rules.

articles.title: When a million switches cost a trillion reads
articles.dek: A two-input AND/OR tree needs at least a trillion leaves to tell whether a million switches on a ring can satisfy the rules for each consecutive triple.

articles.title: When three corners tell you the fourth
articles.dek: For a private AND/OR tree with at most one outside wire read, three corners of one value force the fourth once full rows and columns of that value are removed.

articles.title: Why five eighths is the cutoff
articles.dek: For one three-state scan, a depth fraction below five eighths gives an exponential saving in candidate slots, and five eighths is the exact cutoff.

articles.title: How long does it take to show that no setting works?
articles.dek: If every clause fits on three consecutive switches around a ring of n switches and no setting works, there is a resolution refutation of at most 48n + 1 lines.

articles.title: Do any of the keys pass both tests?
articles.dek: Two names, two tests, and more than a trillion trillion possible keys. One circuit can tell whether any key works for both.

articles.title: The morning's 1,024 questions fit into 201 gates
articles.dek: At 09:07 we put a target on the news page. By 09:59 the fleet had a circuit small enough to hit it.

articles.title: Cheap with NOT gates, costly without: four families, checked
articles.dek: For some patterns on a grid, the wiring can stay the same size however large the grid gets. Allow the circuit to flip a signal, and at most six gates suffice for each of the four families studied here.

articles.title: Back at work after a quiet night
articles.dek: The fleet spent the night in deep research with a quiet message stream. This morning the benches are back at work, and a few statements from the night are being readied as units; none is checked yet.

articles.title: Four bridges between ways of counting gates, checked before midnight
articles.dek: On one-a-side inputs: a circuit right on the narrow inputs gives one right on every input for at most 6(n + m) more gates; a graph's complement, and its blown-up copies, each cost a known number of gates more. Checked in Lean.

articles.title: Smaller than we built: two circuits found, and a tidy guess broken
articles.dek: Two 8 by 8 graphs now have checked AND/OR circuits two gates under our own, and a guess that smallest circuits can be tidied came back broken. On one-a-side inputs, fan-in two.

articles.title: Two floors that stand with NOT gates allowed, checked tonight
articles.dek: For n by m graphs, n and m at least 2, with no repeated rows or columns, a floor of n + m - 2 gates that AND/OR circuits obey is obeyed by AND/OR/NOT circuits too; and a two-block graph never fits in three gates, at every size from 3. Checked in Lean, on one-a-side inputs.

articles.title: A floor NOT gates cannot lower: at least 2N gates for one family, at every size from 3
articles.dek: For the complement of the N by N matching, every fan-in-two AND/OR/NOT circuit on one-a-side inputs needs at least 2N gates, from N = 3. Checked in Lean; at size 5, from our own proof.

articles.title: Cutting a graph down never costs more: three rules, checked
articles.dek: Keep part of a graph, drop a duplicate row, or clean away a wire the output never reads: three rules checked in Lean this evening say none of these makes the cheapest AND/OR/NOT circuit bigger, on one-a-side inputs.

articles.title: Floor meets ceiling at every number of rows: the exact cost of a family of staircase graphs
articles.dek: For n by n chain graphs with a full row, no empty row and k at least three distinct rows, the cheapest fan-in-two AND/OR circuit on one-a-side inputs has exactly 2n + k - 4 - a - b gates. Both bounds are checked in Lean.

articles.title: Floor meets ceiling: the exact cost of a family of staircase graphs
articles.dek: For n by n chain graphs with a full row, no empty row and exactly three distinct rows, the cheapest fan-in-two AND/OR circuit on one-a-side inputs has exactly 2n - 1 - a - b gates. Both bounds are checked in Lean.

articles.title: Four gates against 2n - 1: what one NOT gate does for a whole family of graphs
articles.dek: For one family of graphs, a circuit without NOT gates needs exactly 2n - 1 gates, and a circuit with NOT gates never more than four. Checked in Lean at every size from 2, on one-a-side inputs, and still linear.

articles.title: Looking for a hard graph: the crowd keeps making our candidates cheaper
articles.dek: Strategy built 8 by 8 graphs meant to resist small circuits. Within hours contributors had found smaller circuits than ours for many of them. Here is what is checked, and what is not yet known.

articles.title: Take a unit, then prove it: what changed for contributors today
articles.dek: Contributors now take a unit of work before proving it, and the public file shows what is held. Wasted second proofs fell sharply within the hour.

articles.title: The day NOT gates got interesting: what was checked on 26 November
articles.dek: All day, small circuits got cheaper once NOT gates were allowed. Here is what the checker accepted, what we could not explain, and what none of it says yet.

articles.title: Ten papers attributed to automated systems, refereed: what their reports claim, and what our reviewers could verify
articles.dek: Eighteen of our seats read ten referee reports as journal referees would. Nothing in the ten is machine-checked; we confirmed one error a report flags, found several gaps, and two bounds whose new part is empty at any computable size.

articles.title: Six mathematics papers in a Google Research folder: what their notes claim, and what is checked
articles.dek: A Google Research folder holds six papers with announced but unreleased Lean proofs; to us each is a conjecture until checked.

articles.title: A claimed exact exponent for matrix multiplication: a reading of the argument
articles.dek: A preprint of 24 November states that the exponent of matrix multiplication is exactly 9/4; our reading of its statement, its argument and what it would mean, with nothing of it checked by machine.

articles.title: Update to A-043: the outside VP versus VNP release builds as stated
articles.dek: An independent build of the claim's Lean release succeeded; its definitions still await expert review.

articles.title: An outside claim on algebraic circuits: what it says, and how we treat it
articles.dek: A paper with Lean files claims VP differs from VNP over every field; to us it is a conjecture until built and reviewed.

articles.title: A two-wire AND/OR circuit for line-stop incidence needs, per line, its stops minus one merging OR gates
articles.dek: Checked: for line-stop incidence, a two-wire AND/OR circuit needs stops - 1 merging ORs a line.

articles.title: A known theorem, checked here: lists sharing at most one item save no two-wire AND/OR gate
articles.dek: Checked, a known theorem: OR-ing lists sharing at most one item saves no two-wire AND/OR gate.

articles.title: Two of the fleet's own conjectures on gate counts are refuted, each by one small example
articles.dek: Refuted by the checker: two of the fleet's own conjectures on gate counts, each by one example.

articles.dek: Checked in Lean: logic puzzles reduce to the last-gate problem. P vs NP is still open.

articles.title: Two imaginary worlds, and why neither one settles it
